subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Water Cycle
description: A fast breakdown of The Water Cycle for builders.

hook.text: The water in your glass may once have been inside a dinosaur. Water is endlessly recycled.

buildup.text: The Sun heats ocean water, which evaporates into the atmosphere as invisible vapor.

discovery.text: Vapor condenses into clouds. Clouds drop rain and snow on land, filling rivers and aquifers.

twist.text: Climate change is speeding up the cycle — more evaporation, heavier storms, faster droughts.

climax.text: The total amount of water stays constant. Its distribution is what's shifting.

punchline.text: Earth doesn't lose water. It just moves it to places we don't expect.

quiz.question: How does climate change affect the water cycle?
options: It speeds up evaporation and intensifies storms

details.summary: The water cycle moves water continuously between oceans, atmosphere, and land through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. Solar energy drives evaporation, winds carry moisture across continents, and gravity returns water to oceans via rivers and groundwater flow.
details.whyItMatters: The water cycle distributes freshwater across the planet. Climate change is accelerating and disrupting this cycle, intensifying both droughts and floods in different regions.
takeaways: Evaporation, condensation, and precipitation drive the cycle
Solar energy is the primary engine moving water
Climate change is intensifying the water cycle globally

faq.question: How is climate change affecting the water cycle?
faq.answer: Warmer air holds about seven percent more moisture per degree of warming, intensifying both evaporation and rainfall. This makes wet regions wetter and dry regions drier, increases heavy precipitation events, and accelerates glacial melting that alters seasonal water supply.

faq.question: How long does a water molecule stay in the atmosphere?
faq.answer: The average residence time of water vapor in the atmosphere is about 9 to 10 days. By contrast, deep groundwater can remain underground for thousands of years, and ocean water takes roughly 3,000 years to complete a full cycle.
